clue.text: Side with defensive player

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to support or take the part of someone
second meaning: a full-... or half-... in football or hockey

explanation.surface: A manager picking a team that leans on a defender.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb meaning support a person and a noun for a defending position on a sports team.

clue.text: Crafty way to secure a loan?

definitions.text: Crafty way to secure a loan?

parts.words: Crafty way to secure a loan?
parts.note: surface reading: a cunning trick for getting someone to lend you money
setter's reading: to do with craft, that is ships, so a loan secured on a vessel

explanation.walkthrough: 'Crafty' suggests cunning, but it means relating to boats: the answer is an old maritime loan pledged against a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Bottomry is a historic contract in which a shipowner borrows money using the vessel's hull as security.

clue.text: Business replacing one in second firm

indicators.note: replacing means one item takes the place of another inside the longer word

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a business
I is the Roman numeral for one
an instant is a second, a moment

explanation.surface: A company takes over a single post in another firm.
explanation.walkthrough: In INSTANT, the I is swapped for CO.
explanation.definitionFit: Firm and constant both mean steadfast and unwavering, as in a loyal supporter.

clue.text: Director of a show that could be starring me

indicators.note: 'could be' says the letters that follow might become something else once rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A would-be performer dreams of directing the show that features them.
explanation.walkthrough: The ten letters of 'starring me' rearrange into RINGMASTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A ringmaster is the person who runs and introduces the acts in a circus performance.

clue.text: Transport union that's about to become effective

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the two letters for that is go around the union

parts.note: i.e., id est, means that is
the NUR was the National Union of Railwaymen, a British transport union

explanation.surface: A railway workers' union whose new agreement is about to come into force.
explanation.walkthrough: The NUR was a British rail workers' union. Besides 'accustom', the legal sense of the answer is to take effect.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, a right or provision is said to inure when it takes effect or comes into operation.

clue.text: Chambers surrounded by FBI agents and union supporters

indicators.note: surrounded by means the first item sits inside the second

parts.note: G-men are US federal government agents
chambers are rooms

explanation.surface: Offices raided by federal agents and trade unionists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Union' suggests a trade union, but it is a wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: Groomsmen attend the bridegroom at a wedding, so they support a marriage, the union of two people.

clue.text: Skilled assistant engineer dismissed and cast off

indicators.note: dismissed means sent away, so the engineer's letters are dropped from the helper word

parts.note: an accomplice is an assistant, usually in crime
CE is a civil engineer
to shed is to cast off

explanation.surface: A capable helper is fired along with the engineer and thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: ACCOMPLICE loses CE at its end, leaving ACCOMPLI, then SHED.
explanation.definitionFit: Accomplished describes someone highly trained and expert at an art or activity.

clue.text: Wag starts to tell really unsuitable and naughty tale

indicators.note: starts to means the opening letters of the words that follow are taken

parts.words: tell really unsuitable and naughty tale
parts.note: the first letter of each of these six words

explanation.surface: A joker begins a rude and inappropriate story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wag' looks like a joker, but in British slang to wag school, or a wag, is a child skipping classes.
explanation.definitionFit: In British dialect a wag is a pupil who stays away from school without permission.

clue.text: Come back with lab equipment

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to reply sharply or wittily
second meaning: a glass vessel with a long bent neck used for distilling

explanation.surface: Returning to the laboratory with some apparatus.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a sharp verbal reply and also a long-necked distilling flask used by chemists.

clue.text: Mini — it's going round city

indicators.note: going round means turning about, so the little word it is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
NY is New York, the city

explanation.surface: A small car being driven around town.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mini is a famous small British car, but here the word is the adjective meaning very small.
explanation.definitionFit: Mini as an adjective means very small, a direct synonym for tiny.

clue.text: Some tennis shots are not worth considering

definitions.meaning: first meaning: balls landing beyond the lines of play
second meaning: dismissed without a hearing, as in ruled out

explanation.surface: A coach dismissing certain tennis strokes as worthless.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennis balls hit long land outside the playing area, and a proposal dismissed without discussion is said to be ruled out this way.

clue.text: We left much property for support of the needy

parts.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left
far means much, as in far better
an estate is a landed property

explanation.surface: Someone bequeaths a big estate to charity for the poor.
explanation.definitionFit: The welfare state is a government system of benefits and services that provides for people in need.

clue.text: Opposite middle of ship? Correct!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a nautical bearing at right angles to the keel, level with the widest part of a vessel
second meaning: on the right track, as an aircraft following a radio guidance signal

explanation.surface: A sailor checks a position question and gets it right.
explanation.walkthrough: A ship's beam is its greatest width, amidships; the second sense comes from pilots flying along a radio guide signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both a sailing bearing level with amidships and informal speech for being exactly right.

clue.text: Wander around, taking in new house

indicators.note: around signals turning the word for wander about so it reads backwards
taking in means one word swallows another inside it

parts.note: to roam is to wander
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Strolling round a new home before moving in.
explanation.walkthrough: ROAM backwards gives MAOR, which then holds N in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A manor is a large country house, the main residence of a landed estate.

clue.text: Usual fight sequence?

definitions.meaning: second meaning read literally: a mill is old slang for a fist fight, and a run is a sequence

explanation.surface: Asking whether a film's punch-up is the standard routine.
explanation.walkthrough: Mill is an old boxing word for a bout of fisticuffs, so a run of them is a sequence of fights.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means ordinary or commonplace, like goods straight off the factory line without selection.

clue.text: When the tide's in in Lake Titicaca

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the time when the sea is at its fullest
second meaning read literally: the Andean lake lies about 3,800 metres above sea level, so a swimmer there is in elevated liquid

explanation.surface: Asking about the tides on a famous South American lake.
explanation.walkthrough: Titicaca has no real tide; it is among the world's loftiest navigable lakes, which gives the second, literal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the peak of the tide, and read literally describes a body of water set at great altitude.

clue.text: Tramp featured in paper showing a lot of bottle

indicators.note: featured in means appearing inside, so one word sits within the other

parts.note: a ream is a quantity of paper
a hobo is a tramp

explanation.surface: A vagrant pictured in the newspaper displays great courage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottle' in British slang means nerve, but here it is a real wine bottle of great size.
explanation.definitionFit: A rehoboam is an oversized wine or champagne bottle holding about six standard measures.

clue.text: Runner who's barely visible

parts.note: surface reading: an athlete so fast or distant they can hardly be seen
setter's reading: in the bare, naked, someone who dashes across a public event unclothed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Barely visible' suggests hardly seen, but it means seen bare, without clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a person who runs naked through a crowd or sports ground for attention.

clue.text: Stall in which monster is to be seen in France, without payment

parts.note: a dragon is a fabled monster

indicators.note: without here means outside, so the French word wraps around the money word

parts.words: is to be seen in France
parts.note: est is French for is
a fee is a payment

explanation.surface: A market stall where a monster is shown in France, free of charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stall' looks like a booth, but it is the verb meaning delay. 'Without' is the old sense of outside.
explanation.definitionFit: To stall is to delay deliberately, and the idiom describes acting slowly or reluctantly on purpose.

clue.text: Cat has interminable shivering fit sitting in grate

indicators.note: sitting in means placed inside another word

parts.note: to jar is to grate, as on the nerves

indicators.note: interminable means without end, so the last letter of the illness word is dropped

parts.note: an ague is a fever with shivering fits

explanation.surface: A shivering cat crouches in the fireplace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grate' looks like a fireplace, but it is the verb meaning to rasp or jar.
explanation.definitionFit: The jaguar is a large spotted wild cat of Central and South America.

clue.text: Climbing mountain, policemen appear unflappable

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing means going upwards, so the word for mountain reads from bottom to top

parts.note: an alp is a mountain
the CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, British plain-clothes detectives

explanation.surface: Detectives scaling a peak stay calm.
explanation.definitionFit: Placid and unflappable both describe someone calm and not easily upset or agitated.

clue.text: Set of maps a sailor returned

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: returned means sent back the way it came, so the word for sailor is read backwards

parts.note: an old salt is an experienced sailor

explanation.surface: A seaman brings back the charts he borrowed.
explanation.definitionFit: An atlas is a bound book collecting maps of the world or a region.

clue.text: Looking dismal, having eaten nothing, we plead with somebody

indicators.note: having eaten means taking something inside, so the first word swallows the round letter

parts.note: taken as written
O, the figure zero, means nothing
to beg is to plead
one means a person, somebody

explanation.surface: Hungry and miserable, we implore someone for food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having eaten nothing' reads as hunger in the surface, but it is the instruction to put the zero-shaped letter inside the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Woebegone describes a sad, sorrowful appearance, so it fits a person looking gloomy and dejected.

clue.text: It's scoffed at in mid-teens

indicators.note: in places the little word inside the kept letters
mid means the middle, so only the central letters of the following word are kept

parts.note: the middle three letters of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something young teenagers mock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoffed at' reads as mocked, but 'scoffed' alone is the definition, meaning gobbled.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang to scoff is to eat greedily, so food scoffed has been devoured.

clue.text: Immorality in church, a way to disrupt harmony

indicators.note: to disrupt is to break into, so the earlier letters burst into the middle of the word for harmony

parts.note: unity is harmony, accord
CH is the abbreviation for church
taken as written
ST, street, is a way

explanation.surface: A scandal in a parish upsets the congregation's peace.
explanation.definitionFit: Unchastity is sexual impropriety, one particular form of immoral conduct, so the general word fits.

clue.text: Hit button the wrong way

indicators.note: the wrong way means back to front, so the word for button is read from the end

parts.note: a knob is a button or control

explanation.surface: Pressing the wrong control on a machine.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonk is an informal word for a blow, especially a light knock on the head.

clue.text: Something that can distract and upset herd, straying

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and disordered, so the word herd is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
erring means straying from the right path

explanation.surface: A herding dog disrupts cattle, which wander off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Straying' looks like part of the anagram signal, but it supplies its own synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A red herring is a false clue or diversion meant to lead attention away from the truth.

clue.text: Title to some extent like Mirza

indicators.note: to some extent means only partly, so the answer is a stretch of the following words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A rank that resembles Mirza, a Persian honorific.
explanation.walkthrough: Mirza is itself a Persian title, which makes the surface plausible.
explanation.definitionFit: Emir is an honorific title for a Muslim ruler or commander in the Middle East.
